title: Technocracy Can’t Fix Europe
gist: Alberto Alemanno assesses the newly launched Rhine Group — a private club of European business, financial, and tech elites co-chaired by Mario Draghi and Patrick Collison and aimed at restoring Europe's capacity to innovate, grow, and compete — and warns that it will fail unless it recognizes that the problem it targets is fundamentally political, not technocratic.

insights.claim: The Rhine Group, launched to restore Europe's capacity to innovate, grow, and compete globally, is a private club assembled to do what public institutions are supposed to do.
insights.speaker: ALBERTO ALEMANNO
insights.so_what: A private elite initiative stepping into the void left by EU institutions is a signal of how stalled official European reform has become — worth watching as a channel for competitiveness and capital-markets-union advocacy.
insights.quote: a private club assembled to do what public institutions are supposed to do

insights.claim: The Rhine Group is co-chaired by former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi and tech entrepreneur Patrick Collison, with LSE economist and former MEP Luis Garicano as executive director.
insights.speaker: ALBERTO ALEMANNO
insights.so_what: The heavyweight lineup gives the group real convening power over European policy debate — its agenda on growth and innovation could shape the reform narrative Draghi's competitiveness report already set in motion.
insights.quote: former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi and the tech entrepreneur Patrick Collison serving as co-chairs. Luis Garicano, an LSE economist and former liberal member of the European Parliament, is the executive director.
insights.locator: Nonetheless, it has brought together many household names

insights.claim: The Rhine Group could prove useful in kick-starting European growth and innovation, but only if it recognizes that the problem it hopes to solve is fundamentally political rather than technical.
insights.speaker: ALBERTO ALEMANNO
insights.so_what: Implies that technocratic fixes to Europe's competitiveness gap will underdeliver without political buy-in — tempering expectations for any elite-driven reform push and its market impact.
insights.quote: But first, it must recognize that the problem it hopes to solve is fundamentally political.
